authoring.value:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }10{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}10{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4x}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =10\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4a}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}) \\  & =10\cdot (\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-4a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{-4x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{-4x}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-4x}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/ade58ce56684420fb0f00236af50bbb54f76801fc8870e1cce135cbd51f1b726.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }10{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & =10\cdot (\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-4a}) \\  & =10(\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{4}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}2\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{1}{5}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}]}_{a}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{5}^{x}]}_{a}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({5}^{1}-{5}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (5-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={5}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{5}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{5}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/06c51ecc423683f4377248004b7a318f1348836bd752a7f65f94457d1774e64d.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}2\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (5-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (5-0) \\  & =\frac{10}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

authoring.question: e-10554
authoring.value:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int e^{px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1p e^{px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\,]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-3x}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^{-3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^{-3x} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^{-3x} =0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/bc4ffc41105491f2bd6b37b2482afc64946d8f67f6db83dfa322c400ae4bc2b6.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x} & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (0-{e}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

authoring.value:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int b^{\,px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1{p\ln(b)} b^{\,px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{2}^{2x+1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {2}^{1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{2}^{2x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({2}^{0}-{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=2^{2x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} 2^{2x} = 0$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} 2^{2x} = \infty$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/009f467677932d0ac17e1632c31f4d3aa5271ffe332730d9670e69862b243bef.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

authoring.question: e-10553
authoring.value:
First, we substitute $u=x^4.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 4x^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac 14 \textrm{d}u =x^3\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty$ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^4$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{2}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{2}^{-u}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{2^x},$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = 0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/1969145d74662468ec23d458ac1ad0194d51cbf6b026718b7232466e9357efdf.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$
